bridgeLines: I spent six years as a Navy Communications Electronics Supervisor keeping mission-critical communications and electronics up on a destroyer — same urgency as keeping a pharmacy line running: diagnose fast, restore safely, document everything.
In the Navy I lived in SKED as our CMMS — scheduling maintenance, working packages, spot checks, and closing out work. That is the same work-order discipline Optum wants in CMMS or SAP.
At BAE I followed controlled procedures on electronics repair with strict parts and quality records — that reinforces the CMMS habit from SKED.
I'm comfortable on nights/watches and radio-style priority calls; Communications Electronics Supervisor ownership and ESS supervisor watch prepared me for 2nd-shift service response.
I may not have lived on a pill-packaging OEM every day, but I know how to learn a platform fast, isolate electrical/electronic/mechanical faults, and keep availability high.

personalizedAnswers.q: Walk me through how you troubleshoot a machine that suddenly stops on the line.
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: I'd start with safety — don't chase a running fault if LOTO or an e-stop condition applies. Then I'd define the symptom: alarms, last product, last change, what the HMI/PLC is throwing. On the ship and at BAE I learned to check utilities and inputs before swapping assemblies — power, air if present, sensors/permissives, then isolate electrical vs mechanical vs controls. I'd restore in a controlled way, verify, and close the work order with what I found so the next tech isn't starting from zero. Closest story: CASREP-level TVS/radio faults and the modem/IP restore under pressure.

personalizedAnswers.q: Tell me about a time you diagnosed an electrical / electronics issue.
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: Navy destroyer communications gear — I was the TVS subject-matter tech and helped drive Category II/III casualty corrections on tactical switching and digital radio systems. Method was systematic fault isolation with procedures and test equipment, not guesswork. At BAE I kept that same controlled-procedure habit. I'm honest that my deepest hours are electronics/communications systems and shipboard electrical supervision, and I'm ready to ramp on their specific 480V motor-control and pharmacy OEM prints.

personalizedAnswers.q: How do you use CMMS or SAP day to day?
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: In the Navy I used SKED as our CMMS every day as a Communications Electronics Supervisor — scheduling preventive maintenance, working packages, doing spot checks, and closing out corrective jobs so the record matched reality. I also ran repair-parts support for two divisions — requisitions over $1.5M and about $126K saved by cleaning up inventory — plus BAE maintenance/parts/quality records. I haven't lived in SAP daily, but SKED gave me real CMMS habits: the work order is the source of truth for problem, cause, parts, time, and follow-up. I'll map that straight onto whatever CMMS or SAP Charlotte uses.

personalizedAnswers.q: Tell me about your leadership / supervisor experience.
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: I was a Communications Electronics Supervisor in the Navy — owning work-center priorities, training technicians, and keeping communications electronics available for the ship. That meant assigning work, checking quality, using SKED to stay ahead of maintenance, and answering high-priority casualties without losing the schedule. Later as a survey Crew Chief I led field crews the same way: clear assignments, safety, and communication when something blocked the job.

personalizedAnswers.q: Have you worked with Allen-Bradley / Studio 5000?
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: Be honest: I have PLC exposure from Navy electronics maintenance competencies and I'm comfortable reading control logic, I/O, and HMI alarms conceptually, but I will not oversell Studio 5000 hours I don't have. Pivot: I'm a trained electronics tech who learns platforms quickly, and I want to know which AB/Beckhoff assets are on the Charlotte line so I can prioritize that in onboarding.

personalizedAnswers.q: This role is Sun–Thu 2nd shift with occasional Saturday OT. Are you flexible?
personalizedAnswers.yourAnswer: Yes — say it clearly. Navy watchstanding and deployment operations mean I'm used to nights, weekends, and showing up when the mission needs coverage. Confirm Sun–Thu 1400–2330 and occasional Saturday mornings work for you.

I want back onto equipment that matters when it goes down. Navy/BAE taught me that availability protects the mission; here availability protects patients getting medications. Charlotte is workable from my NC base, 2nd shift fits how I already work, and the mix of electrical, electronics, and automation is where I do my best work.
